summary:
TerraNexus is a hackathon project (Gliwice 2026) with interactive 3D globes of Mars and the Moon. Users rotate, zoom and click any location. They get an orbital photo popup and a details panel with terrain data and matching Earth analogues.

Imagery and elevation come from NASA Trek tiles. For Mars these are the Viking colour mosaic (232 m/px), MOLA elevation (463 m/px) and THEMIS infrared (100 m/px). For the Moon they are LROC WAC (100 m/px) and LOLA elevation. Relief is exaggerated 1–8×, and lighting and shadows are computed in the browser. Popup photos come from the NASA Image and Video Library, and planetary figures from NASA Fact Sheets.

The Earth-matching engine is computed rather than typed by hand. A grid of 226,361 points at 0.25° (~28 km) combines NASA POWER climate and dust (AOD_55) data with relief and slope derived from NOAA ETOPO 2022 (60 arc-second, ~450 MB). Nine variables per point are ranked by a fixed hierarchy, returning five distinct sites at least 250 km apart. Macrostrat geology is fetched live for about 40 top candidates.

A FastAPI backend proxies NASA data, and about 720 cached tiles speed up repeat visits.

Artificial intelligence (Claude, by Anthropic) was used to improve the website’s visual quality: layout, styling and the interactive globes.
details: TerraNexus is an interactive 3D globe of Mars and the Moon built from real NASA imagery and elevation data. You click any spot and get an orbital photo plus terrain, climate and geology details. Then it finds the five best matching places on Earth, at least 250 km apart, by comparing that spot with a computed grid of 226,361 Earth points. Conditions that can’t be recreated in a lab, like dust, relief, slope and rock type, count the most, while things you can set in a test chamber, like temperature and light, count the least. This helps researchers, students and mission teams choose realistic, cheaper test sites for rovers, habitats and training. It’s creative because it goes beyond a map and ranks Earth sites by what a lab can’t simulate, with real elevation driving the 3D relief and shadows. We built it with JavaScript, three.js, GLSL, Python and FastAPI on a normal laptop, using data from NASA, NOAA and Macrostrat. We considered data accuracy, speed, NASA’s rate limits and ease of setup, and we listed every source in the app.
